newsitem.title: JAPAN: Barclays aims for profile in Japan fixed income.
newsitem.headline: Barclays aims for profile in Japan fixed income.

text.p: The Barclays Group aims to be a top foreign player in Tokyo's fixed income market by early next year and is also keen to cash in on the expected growth in Japan's mutual fund business, a top executive says.

"We intend to be one of the top five or six foreign players in this market place," Andrew Simmonds, president of BZW Securities (Japan) Ltd, told Reuters in an interview this week, adding that the firm's recent push to boost its fixed income operations had begun from a "virtual standstill".

BZW Securities (Japan), an investment bank belonging to the Barclays Group, has already taken steps to expand its fixed income operations -- such as government bonds -- including a commitment announced in late September to boost its capital to 43 billion yen ($377 million) with an injection of 31 billion yen ($271 million) from British-based parent Barclays PLC.

"One of the gaps we identified very early on was an inadequate presence in fixed income domestically," Simmonds said. "Without plugging that gap, we were holding back a number of other product areas, particularly derivatives, and we were presenting a face to the market where we were perceived as not full spectrum."
Following a recruitment drive and the capital rise, which is being implemented in stages, BZW expects its Japan fixed income operations to be at "full capacity" by the first quarter of 1997, he said.

The Barclays Group -- including BZW Securities Japan, Barclays Bank, Barclays Trust and Banking Company (Japan) Ltd, BZW Investment Management (Japan) Ltd and BZW Nikko Global Investors -- now has about 560 employees in Japan, up from about 530 a year ago. "We see that going to nearly 600 over the next 18 months to two years," Simmonds said.

He said the relatively high volatility of Japan's bond market, due partly to its narrow range of debt series, boosted profit opportunities, but added that should that change, BZW would remain committed to the market.
"It's not so much that we're looking to make bundles of money just from being in the debt market. We needed that capability to develop our other business," he said.
Barclays Group is also hoping to cash in on expected growth in Japan's mutual fund, or unit trust, business.
"One of the things I think is exciting is the potential mutualisation of the savings base in Japan. We're not alone there -- everyone else is excited by that," Simmonds said.

"The interesting thing is the sudden alarm over the ageing population which is leading think tanks inside government to realise one way they can alleviate the problem is to shift some of the...support structure that needs to be in place...back onto the consumer," he said.
"You'll only get them to do that if you provide them with a broader range of savings products."
While direct sales of mutual funds would be possible for firms with high brand recognition, others might have to "piggy back" on domestic firms' distribution networks, he added.

Some foreign investment trusts sell their funds directly in Japan, but most are sold through Japanese brokerages' retail networks. A mutual fund pools together money from many investors to establish a diversified portfolio. Investors receive dividends in proportion to their holdings.
Simmonds also said Barclays expects proposed deregulation of Japan's financial markets to create new opportunities by tearing down barriers among different financial sectors.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto announced earlier this month sweeping proposals for a Japanese-style "Big Bang" to open up Tokyo's financial markets by the year 2001.
"Some of those trip wires being taken down -- that would open up a lot of opportunities for structuring different products across asset management, derivatives, retail mutual funds," Simmonds said.
